cues.x: Man's Search for Meaning, by Viktor E. Frankl.
I want to start with a small object on a table in an apartment in Vienna, in the year 1941, because everything that follows turns on it.

Viktor Frankl was thirty six years old, a neurologist and psychiatrist, the head of the neurology department at the Rothschild Hospital, which was at that time the only hospital in Vienna still permitted to admit Jewish patients.
He had already spent years developing his own school of psychotherapy.
He had a manuscript.
He had a career ahead of him.
And he had, that year, something that was almost impossible to obtain: an American visa.
A way out.
The problem was his parents.
The visa was for him.
It did not cover them.
If he left, they would remain in Vienna, elderly, and by then nobody had any real illusions about what was coming.
So he walked around the city trying to decide, and he went into St Stephen's Cathedral, and he asked, in whatever way a person asks such a thing, for a sign.
When he got home, he found a small piece of marble lying on the table.
He asked his father what it was.
His father said he had picked it up that day from the site of one of Vienna's largest synagogues, which the National Socialists had burned down.
It was a fragment of the stone tablets that had held the Ten Commandments.
His father said he could identify, from the single Hebrew letter engraved on it, which commandment it came from.
There was only one commandment that began with that letter.
Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land.
Frankl stayed.
He let the visa expire.
In 1942 he was deported with his wife Tilly and his parents to Theresienstadt.
His father died there.
He was later transported to Auschwitz, then to two camps connected to Dachau.
Over the next three years he was in four camps.
His mother was killed at Auschwitz.
His brother was killed.
His wife, who was pregnant when they were taken, and who had been forced to abort the child, died at Bergen-Belsen, not long before that camp was liberated.
Of his immediate family, only his sister, who had emigrated to Australia, survived.
He was liberated in April 1945.
He came back to Vienna and learned, one by one, that everybody was dead.
And then, in 1946, in nine consecutive days, dictating to three secretaries in shifts, he wrote this book.
He intended to publish it anonymously.
He did not want his name on it.
He thought of it as a case study, not a memoir, and he was faintly embarrassed by the personal material.
Friends persuaded him to put his name on the cover at the last moment.

It has since sold many millions of copies in dozens of languages, and when the Library of Congress once surveyed readers about the books that had most changed their lives, this one came near the top of the list.
Frankl himself was always slightly bewildered by that, and he said something about it that I think is the right way into the whole book.

He said that if a book written by a man whose own family was destroyed, a book that makes no promises and offers no consolation, could be read by millions as a source of hope, then it must speak to a need in people that nothing else was addressing.
So let me take you through it properly.
The book has two halves and they are completely different in texture.
The first half is his account of the camps, written not as history but as a psychiatrist's observation of what happens to the human mind under total deprivation.
The second half is the theory that came out of it, which he called logotherapy.
I will do both, and I will spend most of the time on the first, because that is where the argument is actually made.
He begins by warning you what this book is not.
It is not an account of the great horrors, which he says have been described often enough by people better placed to describe them.
It is about the small torments of ordinary prisoners.

It is deliberately written from the inside, from the position of the man in the ranks rather than the historian afterwards, and Frankl says explicitly that the ones who were there are not necessarily the ones best qualified to judge, because, and here is a line that hangs over everything, we who have come back know: the best of us did not return.
He then organises what he saw into three psychological phases, and I want to give you each one because the structure is the argument.
Phase one is the period of admission, and its dominant emotion is shock.
His transport arrives at Auschwitz after days in a cattle truck.
The train slows.
Someone at a small window reads out the name of the station.
Fifteen hundred people had left, packed eighty to a carriage, sleeping on their luggage and the little straw on the floor.
Now they file out into searchlights and shouting.
And then comes the moment Frankl describes with a strange flat precision, because it happened in about two seconds and it decided everything.
A senior officer stood at the head of the line.
As each man came before him, the officer looked at him briefly and made a small casual movement with his index finger, pointing left or right.
Not a decision made with any visible weight.
A gesture, repeated hundreds of times, the way you might wave away a fly.
Frankl was sent to the right.
He did not know what either direction meant.
He learned that evening.
Roughly nine in ten of the men from his transport had been sent the other way, and the other way led directly to the crematorium.
He asked an older prisoner where a colleague of his had been taken.
The prisoner pointed at a chimney several hundred yards away, where a flame was rising, and said, that is where your friend is, floating up to heaven.
They were stripped of everything.
Frankl had, sewn into the lining of his coat, the manuscript of his first book, the work of years, the entire scientific case for the ideas he had built his life around.
He tried to plead for it.
He was told, in an obscene word, exactly what would happen to it.
Everything was taken: clothes, hair, every hair on the body, names.
He was given a number.
In the camps, he says, you become a number, and a number that is either fit to work or not, and nothing else about you is of the slightest interest to anyone.
Then they were herded into a shower room, and here is where Frankl notices something psychologically remarkable.
Nobody knew whether water or gas would come out of those pipes.
And what he observed in himself and in the men around him was not, mostly, terror.
It was a bleak, absurd humour.
Men made jokes while they waited.
He describes it as the soul's weapon in the fight for self preservation, humour as a small, defiant act of distance from the situation.
Alongside the humour was something he names the delusion of reprieve.
It is the condemned man's conviction, right up until the final instant, that he will somehow be pardoned.
On arrival almost every prisoner clings to some version of it.
Perhaps this camp is not that bad.
Perhaps my skills will be needed.
Perhaps my case is different.
And this phase ends, usually within days, when curiosity replaces terror and then a flat wonder sets in.
Frankl notes with a doctor's eye that men who had suffered for years from chronic conditions found their symptoms gone.

Men who had never gone a night without medication slept in freezing huts on bare boards, nine to a bed the width of about six and a half feet, without a coat, having handed their shoes over, and did not die of it.
He remarks, with grim scientific interest, that the textbooks lie: a human being can bear vastly more than the textbooks claim.
Phase two is apathy, and it is the long middle of the experience.
Frankl describes it as a kind of emotional death, and he does not describe it as a failure.
He describes it as necessary armour.
In the beginning, a prisoner who saw a man beaten, or watched the sick being loaded for the gas chambers, felt it.
After a few weeks he felt very little.
He could stand and watch things that would once have made him ill and feel nothing except a distant, procedural interest.
He gives an example that shows exactly how far this goes.
He is treating patients in a camp hut.
A twelve year old boy is brought in whose feet, having been outside in the snow without shoes, are frozen, and the doctor is picking away the dead tissue, black, gangrenous, piece by piece.
And Frankl notes that he watched this without disgust, without horror, without pity in the ordinary sense, and that this deadening was the only reason he could function at all.
He is honest about what else the apathy produced.
The dominant thought of every waking hour was food.
Men talked about food constantly, described meals in detail, planned menus.
Frankl noticed a rule about this: those who worked the hardest talked about food the least, because they could not spare the energy.
Sex barely featured, which he notes as clinically interesting, since it contradicted the psychoanalytic assumption of his era that the sexual drive would surface under stress.
In a starving man, it simply switches off.
He also describes the cruelties of the internal hierarchy, and he refuses to make it comfortable.
The Capos, prisoners who supervised other prisoners, were often more brutal than the guards, because their position depended on demonstrating brutality.
And he says something that people quote badly, so let me give it carefully.

He says that the ordinary prisoner who survived a long time in the camps, and who came out of it, if he was honest, would have to admit that survival often depended on doing things he was not proud of, on being lucky, on being in the right column, on someone else's number being called instead of his.
He is not making a claim about who deserved to live.
He is saying that survival was very largely not a moral achievement, and that anyone who pretends otherwise was not there.
And he describes suicide.
Every prisoner, he says, considered it, at least fleetingly, and the method was standard enough to have its own phrase: running into the wire, meaning touching the electrified fence.
Frankl says he made himself a promise early on that he would never run into the wire.
Not out of optimism.
Out of a decision that the manner of his ending would remain, insofar as anything remained, his.
Now, into the middle of that apathy, Frankl places the three or four experiences that are the reason this book exists.
The first happens on a march to a work site before dawn.

The men are stumbling in the dark on ice, in the wind, prodded by rifle butts, and the man next to Frankl says, through his collar, something about their wives, and hopes his own does not know what conditions they are in.
And Frankl finds his mind going to his wife.
He does not know if she is alive.
He has no idea and no way to find out.
And he discovers, walking in the dark, that this does not matter to the experience he is having.
He sees her with extraordinary clarity.
He talks to her.
She answers.

And he understands, for the first time as a lived fact rather than a poetic idea, what he had read all his life and never really taken in: that love goes beyond the physical person of the beloved, that it finds its deepest meaning in the spiritual being, and that whether that person is present, or absent, or even alive, somehow ceases to be the central point.
He says it in one sentence that he then spends the rest of his life elaborating.
The salvation of man is through love and in love.
A man who has nothing left in this world may still know bliss, be it only for a brief moment, in the contemplation of his beloved.
The second experience is a bird.
He is digging in a trench, exhausted, in grey light, and a bird flies down and settles on the mound of earth he has just thrown up, and looks steadily at him.
That is all.
He records it because in that moment it did not feel like nothing.
The third is a sunset.
The men are lying in the mud of the hut floor after work, finished, when one of them bursts in and calls them outside to look.

And they stumble out and stand there, in their rags, and watch the sky over Bavaria turn through iron grey and then to a burning red, and someone says, after a long silence, how beautiful the world could be.
And the fourth is not an experience but an arrangement.
Frankl and a friend made a pact that every day, each of them would invent one funny story about something that would happen to them after liberation.
It was a deliberate training programme in humour.
He gives an example.
They imagined that one of them, at some elegant dinner party years later, would forget himself and shout at the hostess in the exact voice of the camp cook ladling soup: dip in.

They practised finding the ridiculous, on purpose, as an exercise, because Frankl believed that the ability to place any distance at all between yourself and your situation was the single skill that most reliably kept a man human.
Which brings me to the central passage of the whole book, and I want to give it to you nearly whole, because it is the sentence around which everything else turns.
Frankl writes that the experience of camp life shows that man does have a choice of action.
He describes the men who walked through the huts comforting others, giving away their last piece of bread.
There were few of them, he says, but they were enough.
They offer sufficient proof that everything can be taken from a man but one thing, the last of the human freedoms: to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.
Note what he is and is not claiming.
He is not claiming that attitude saves you.
It very obviously did not save the men who gave away their bread.
He is not claiming suffering is good, and he specifically attacks that idea later.

He is making a much narrower and much harder claim: that even when literally every other option has been removed, one option remains, and it is not nothing, because it decides who the person is at the end.
He puts it in terms of a spiritual freedom which cannot be taken away, and he says that this is what makes life meaningful and purposeful.
And then he names the mechanism that determines who keeps it.
He quotes Nietzsche, twice, and it is the same line both times because it is the engine of his whole psychiatry: he who has a why to live can bear with almost any how.
Then he gives the evidence, and this is where the book stops being philosophy and becomes something closer to clinical data.
He observed, as a doctor in the camps, that the men who lost their grip on a future died.
Not metaphorically.
Physically.
He watched it happen and he traced the mechanism.
A prisoner who let go of the future let go of his spiritual hold.
He would refuse to get up in the morning.
He would lie in his own filth.
He would not respond to threats.

Often he would take out his hidden cigarettes, the ones that functioned as camp currency and were normally traded for soup, and smoke them, and the other prisoners knew, when they saw a man smoking his own cigarettes, that he had decided to die, and that he would be dead in about forty eight hours.
And he was.
Frankl gives two specific cases.
The first is a fellow prisoner, a composer and librettist, who told him in February 1945 that he had had a dream.
In the dream a voice told him he could ask anything and it would be answered, and he asked when the war would end for him.
The voice said the thirtieth of March.
He told Frankl this in early March, full of hope.
As March wore on and the news from the front made it clear that liberation was not going to arrive by that date, the man's hope began to fail.
On the twenty ninth of March he became suddenly ill with a high fever.
On the thirtieth of March, the day the war was supposed to end for him, he lost consciousness.
On the thirty first he died, of typhus.
Frankl's reading is medical, not mystical.
The camp was full of typhus.

What determined who succumbed was, in a great many cases, the state of the man's immune resistance, and the sudden collapse of hope and courage produced a corresponding collapse of the body's defences.
The dream did not kill him.
The loss of his future did.
The second case is a statistic.
The death rate in one camp rose sharply in the week between Christmas 1944 and New Year 1945, beyond anything explicable by the weather, the rations, the work, or new epidemics.
The reason, Frankl says, was that a large number of prisoners had been living on the naive hope that they would be home by Christmas.
As the days passed and it became evident that they would not be, courage failed on a mass scale, and the bodies followed.
Which is why Frankl, at the darkest point of his own camp experience, gave a speech.
He describes it in detail.
It is the end of a long, terrible day, in a dark hut, no lights, morale destroyed after a death and a wave of illness, men lying on the boards not speaking.
The senior block warden asks Frankl to say something.
So he stood up and, badly and hoarsely, he tried to give them a future.
He talked first about the present, and he did not lie about it.

He said their situation was serious, that he estimated their chances of survival at something like one in twenty, but that he had no intention of abandoning hope, because nobody knew what the next hours would bring, and the front might reach them at any moment.
Then he did something psychologically brilliant.
He talked about the past.
He said that everything they had already lived, all of it, the work they had done, the things they had loved, the suffering they had endured, all of it existed and could never be undone.
Having been is a kind of being, and perhaps the surest kind.
Nothing that has happened can be taken away.
That is a strange comfort, but for men who had lost every material thing, it was the only property they still owned.
Then he talked about sacrifice, and said that if their deaths were coming, the meaning of them would depend on the attitude with which they went, and that this at least was still theirs to decide.
And finally he said that someone was looking down on each of them.
A friend, or a wife, or someone dead, or God.
And that whoever it was, that person would expect not to find them suffering pitifully but to find them suffering proudly, and knowing how to die.
He records the effect plainly.
When the lights came on, he saw men limping towards him with tears in their eyes to thank him.

And he adds, characteristically, that he had to force himself to do it, that on most days he was too exhausted and too frozen to say anything at all, and that he only managed it on very rare occasions.
Now, the great reversal, which is the intellectual heart of the book.
Frankl says that what was ultimately needed was a fundamental change in our attitude towards life.
We had to learn ourselves, and then teach the despairing men, that it did not really matter what we expected from life, but rather what life expected from us.
Stop asking what you want out of life.
Life is asking you.
Every hour and every situation puts a question to a person, and the person answers it, not with words or with meditation, but with what he actually does.
Frankl calls this responsibility, and he keeps splitting the word to show what he means: response, and ability.
The ability to respond.
And the questions are always specific.
There is no general meaning of life in the abstract, he insists, any more than there is a best move in chess in the abstract.
There is only the best move for this position, for this player, at this moment.
Meaning is not a theory.
It is a task, and it differs from man to man and from hour to hour.
He gives two clinical cases from inside the camp, which are the first recorded instances of him doing therapy in that setting.
Two men had told him, separately, that they intended to kill themselves.
Both used exactly the same formula: I have nothing more to expect from life.
Frankl's approach with each of them was to turn the sentence around and ask what life still expected of them, and then to make it concrete, because the abstract version is useless.
For the first man, it was a child.
He had a child abroad, waiting for him, whom he adored.
The child existed.
The child was expecting him.
The second danger is disillusionment.
A man survives, and returns, and finds that the thing he had built the entire architecture of his survival around is gone.
Frankl describes coming home and having to learn, in stages, that everyone was dead.
And he describes the more ordinary shock: the returning man who expected the world to receive him and finds a shrug.

He describes a released prisoner who says, bitterly, that when he got back he found nobody, that the people he had come home for were not there, and worse, the people who were there had no idea what he had been through and did not particularly want to hear it.
Nobody was waiting.

Frankl says the crowning experience for the returning prisoner, when it finally comes, is the day he looks back on everything that happened and finds that he can no longer understand how he endured it, and realises that he now need fear nothing in the world any more, except his God.
Now let me take you into the second half of the book, the theory, because it is short and it converts everything above into something usable.
Frankl called his approach logotherapy, from the Greek word logos, meaning meaning.
It became known as the third Viennese school of psychotherapy, and he positioned it by contrast with the two that came before it in that same city.
Freud, he said, built on the will to pleasure.
Adler built on the will to power.
Frankl proposed that the primary drive in a human being is neither of those.
It is the will to meaning, the striving to find and fulfil a meaning in one's life.
And he pointed out, on the evidence of the camps, that in extreme conditions the will to pleasure and the will to power do not sustain anybody.
The will to meaning does.
He introduced a term for the sickness he was seeing in prosperous post war patients: the existential vacuum.
It is the feeling of an inner emptiness, of a great nothing at the centre.
And he explained its origin structurally.
Unlike an animal, no instinct now tells a human what he must do.
And unlike people in earlier centuries, no tradition tells him what he ought to do.
So, he says, he either does what other people do, which is conformism, or he does what other people tell him to do, which is totalitarianism.
Its chief symptom is boredom, and Frankl argued that boredom was already causing psychiatry more problems than distress.

He named a specific presentation of it: Sunday neurosis, the low, anxious depression that arrives when the working week ends and the busyness stops and a person is left alone with a life that has no content.
He connected it directly to alcoholism, to compulsive behaviour, and to a great deal of depression that gets treated as a chemical problem when it is at least partly a problem of empty meaning.
The crucial claim: he insisted that existential frustration is not itself a neurosis.
A person distressed about the worthwhileness of their life is not thereby ill.
To treat that distress as pathology is a category error.
He was blunt that a certain degree of tension, the gap between what a person is and what they still ought to become, is not only normal but necessary for mental health.
What man needs, he wrote, is not a tensionless state but the striving and struggling for some goal worthy of him.
Then, the practical core: how do you actually find meaning?
Frankl says it is not invented but detected, and that it can be discovered in three ways.
First, by creating a work or doing a deed.
Achievement, contribution, the thing you make or build or accomplish.
Second, by experiencing something or encountering someone.

Beauty, nature, culture, and above all love, which he defines as the only way of grasping another human being in the innermost core of his personality, seeing the potential in them that is not yet actualised, and by seeing it, helping to make it real.
Third, and this is his distinctive contribution, by the attitude we take towards unavoidable suffering.
When we are no longer able to change a situation, he writes, we are challenged to change ourselves.
And here comes the story that, for a lot of readers, is the moment the whole book snaps into focus.
An elderly general practitioner came to Frankl with a severe depression.
His wife, whom he had loved above all else, had died two years earlier, and he could not overcome it.
Frankl did not offer advice or reassurance.
He asked one question.
He said, what would have happened, doctor, if you had died first, and your wife had survived you?
The old man said, oh, for her that would have been terrible.
How she would have suffered.
And Frankl said, you see, doctor, such a suffering has been spared her, and it was you who spared her this suffering.
But now you have to pay for it by surviving and mourning her.
The man said nothing, shook Frankl's hand, and left.
Frankl notes that no words were said, no technique applied, nothing was cured in the medical sense, and the suffering was not reduced by one gram.
What changed was that it now had a meaning.
It was the price of a sacrifice he had made for the woman he loved.
And Frankl's line is: suffering ceases to be suffering at the moment it finds a meaning, such as the meaning of a sacrifice.
But he then puts a hard fence around this, and it matters, because his ideas are frequently abused.
He says clearly: suffering is not necessary to find meaning.
If the suffering is avoidable, the meaningful thing to do is to remove the cause.
Unnecessary suffering, he says, is masochism rather than heroism.
Nobody is required to seek out pain.
The teaching applies only to suffering that cannot be escaped.
He also offers a genuine clinical technique that has outlived him and is still used, called paradoxical intention.
Its basis is the observation that anticipatory anxiety produces exactly what it fears.
A man afraid of blushing blushes.
A man afraid of failing to sleep stays awake because he is trying so hard.

Frankl adds a partner concept, hyper-intention, the fact that things like sleep, pleasure and potency are by-products which disappear the moment they are pursued directly, and hyper-reflection, the excessive self observation that makes it worse.
So the technique is to invert the wish.
The patient is instructed to try, humorously, to produce the very thing they dread.
His favourite example: a young doctor with a terrible fear of sweating.
Any time he expected to sweat, the anticipation triggered it and he would be drenched.
Frankl told him that whenever this happened he should resolve to show the people around him just how much he could sweat.
He should say to himself, I only sweated a quart before, but now I am going to pour out at least ten quarts.
Within one week he had freed himself from a phobia he had carried for four years.
The insomniac is told to try to stay awake as long as possible.
The obsessive is told to wish for the thing they fear.
And the mechanism, Frankl says, is that the humour creates distance, and the distance breaks the loop, because you cannot fear something you are actively trying to achieve.
Underneath the technique sits his general instruction about success, which is the same principle in everyday clothes.
Do not aim at success, he says.
The more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it, because success, like happiness, cannot be pursued.
It must ensue as the unintended side effect of one's personal dedication to a cause greater than oneself.
Forget about it, and it will come.
In his later writing he added the idea of tragic optimism, which is his answer to the obvious objection.
He names the tragic triad that no life escapes: pain, guilt, and death.
And he asks whether it is possible to say yes to life in spite of all three.
His answer is that it is, if you can do three conversions.
Turn suffering into a human achievement.
Derive from guilt the opportunity to change yourself for the better.
And take from life's transitoriness an incentive to act responsibly now.
That last one, transitoriness, gives him one of his most beautiful images.
People look at the passing of time and see only the stubble field of what is gone.
Frankl says they fail to see the full granaries of the past, into which they have already brought the harvest of their lives: the deeds done, the loves lived, the sufferings borne bravely.
None of that can be undone by anything that comes later.
Having been is the surest kind of being there is.
And to make that operational, he offers what may be the most useful single sentence he ever wrote as a rule for daily conduct.
Live as if you were living already for the second time, and as if you had acted the first time as wrongly as you are about to act now.
Two more things before I close, because they show you the man rather than the theory.
The first is what he says about the camps and human nature.
He rejected any notion of collective guilt, firmly and publicly, at a time when it would have been extremely easy for him to do otherwise, and he lectured on it in Germany after the war.
His position was that guilt is personal, never inherited, never collective.
And he wrote the sentence that is, for many readers, the summary of everything he learned.
He said that there are two races of men in this world, and only these two: the race of the decent man and the race of the indecent man.
Both are found everywhere.
They penetrate into all groups of society.
No group consists entirely of decent or indecent people.
And in the same spirit: man is that being who invented the gas chambers of Auschwitz.
However, he is also that being who entered those gas chambers upright, with the Lord's Prayer or the Shema Yisrael on his lips.
The second is his advice about how to treat people, which he borrowed from an aviation analogy.
A pilot flying to a destination in a crosswind, he said, has to aim above and beyond the point he actually wants to reach, otherwise the wind pushes him below it.
And so with human beings.
If we take man as he is, we make him worse.
But if we take him as he should be, we make him capable of becoming what he can be.

He also liked to say that America had a Statue of Liberty on the east coast, and that it should be supplemented by a Statue of Responsibility on the west, because freedom without responsibility degenerates into mere arbitrariness.
Frankl lived to ninety two.
He earned a pilot's licence at sixty seven.
He climbed mountains into old age.
He wrote more than thirty books.

He remarried, had a daughter, and by all accounts was a warm, funny, slightly impatient man who disliked being treated as a saint and objected strongly to being told that his message was that suffering is good.
It is not his message.
His message is that suffering happens, and that its meaning is the one thing about it you can still determine.
So, what do you actually do with this?
First, change the question.

Whenever you catch yourself asking what you are getting out of your life, or your work, or a relationship, deliberately reverse it and ask what is being asked of you here, right now, in this specific situation.
It is not a sentimental exercise.
It usually produces an obvious and slightly inconvenient answer, which is how you know it is working.
Second, find your uniqueness and make it concrete.
Ask what depends on you that would not be done, or not be done in the same way, if you were not here.
A person, a piece of work, a responsibility.
Write it down as a name or a task, not as a category.
That is the answer to the why that lets you bear the how.
Third, when you cannot change a situation, deliberately turn the attention to what you can still choose about your response to it.
Not as a way of pretending it is fine, but as a way of retaining the one thing that cannot be taken.
Fourth, if you are suffering something that is avoidable, remove the cause.
Frankl is emphatic about this and it is the part people skip.
Fifth, if you are caught in a loop of anticipatory anxiety, try paradoxical intention.
Try, with as much humour as you can manage, to produce the very thing you fear.
Aim to blush spectacularly, to lie awake all night, to give the most nervous presentation ever given.
The absurdity creates the distance, and the distance breaks the circuit.
Sixth, stop chasing happiness or success directly.
Both are side effects.
Pick something outside yourself, a cause, a person, a piece of work, and dedicate yourself to it, and let the rest arrive by itself.
And seventh, when you look back at your life and see only what is gone, remember the granaries.
Everything you have already done and loved and endured is stored, permanently, and cannot be taken back by anything the future does.
That is the ground you stand on.
Frankl was asked, over and over, for the meaning of life, and he always refused to answer, because he thought the question was wrong.

What he offered instead was this: everything can be taken from a man but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.
He earned the right to say that in a place where everything else had, in fact, been taken.
